prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the mortgage-underwriting agent (residential mortgage applications and remortgages) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: joint mortgage applicants. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 0)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When one applicant is paid weekly and the other monthly, I should normalise both incomes to the same basis before I test affordability, so I do not overstate or understate the household’s true capacity."},{"type":"fact","content":"When joint applicants do not split household bills evenly, I should use the actual contribution pattern rather than assume a 50/50 split, because affordability depends on what each person really pays."},{"type":"observation","content":"When one applicant has a much stronger credit profile than the other, I should still assess the pair as a single borrowing unit, because the weaker file can determine the overall outcome."},{"type":"preference","content":"When a joint application includes a non-earning or lower-earning applicant, I prefer to check whether their inclusion is needed for lending reasons or only for ownership reasons, as that changes how I evidence the case."},{"type":"fact","content":"When applicants are married, in a civil partnership, or simply cohabiting, I should not assume shared finances are organised the same way; I need to verify how they actually manage income, bills, and savings."},{"type":"observation","content":"When one applicant has variable overtime, bonus, or commission and the other has stable pay, I should look at the combined income pattern over time, not just the latest payslip, to avoid a misleading affordability picture."},{"type":"preference","content":"When a joint remortgage is being used to consolidate debts, I prefer to confirm which debts belong to which applicant and whether both are liable, so the proposed borrowing matches the real liability being cleared."},{"type":"fact","content":"When one applicant is new to the UK credit system or has limited file depth, I should not treat the absence of history as a clean credit profile; I need to look for alternative evidence and any signs of undeclared commitments."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the applicants’ stated future plans differ, such as one expecting parental leave or reduced hours, I should test the affordability against the more cautious scenario, because joint income risk is a shared risk."},{"type":"preference","content":"When documents or declarations do not line up between joint applicants, I prefer to pause and reconcile the inconsistencies first, because small mismatches in names, addresses, or commitments often point to a wider disclosure issue."}]}
